```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)

data_dir <- "datasets"

read_singstat_wide <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE)

  header_index <- which(
    stringr::str_detect(lines, "^Data\\s*Series\\s*,")
  )[1]

  if (is.na(header_index)) {
    stop("No 'Data Series' header found in: ", path)
  }

  raw <- readr::read_csv(
    path,
    skip = header_index - 1,
    na = c("", "na", "NA", "N.A.", "-"),
    show_col_types = FALSE
  )

  raw <- dplyr::rename_with(raw, trimws)
  names(raw)[1] <- "data_series"

  raw |>
    mutate(data_series = stringr::str_squish(data_series)) |>
    filter(!is.na(data_series), data_series != "")
}

to_long_years <- function(data) {
  data |>
    mutate(across(matches("^\\d{4}$"), as.character)) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = matches("^\\d{4}$"),
      names_to = "year",
      values_to = "value"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      year = as.integer(year),
      value = readr::parse_number(as.character(value))
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(year))
}

standardise_age_group <- function(x) {
  x |>
    stringr::str_squish() |>
    stringr::str_replace_all("\\s*-\\s*", "-")
}

age_groups <- c(
  "15-19 Years",
  "20-24 Years",
  "25-29 Years",
  "30-34 Years",
  "35-39 Years",
  "40-44 Years",
  "45-49 Years"
)

age_group_colours <- c(
  "15-19 Years" = "#D73027",
  "20-24 Years" = "#FC8D59",
  "25-29 Years" = "#FEE08B",
  "30-34 Years" = "#91CF60",
  "35-39 Years" = "#1A9850",
  "40-44 Years" = "#4575B4",
  "45-49 Years" = "#7B3294"
)

fertility_wide <- read_singstat_wide(file.path(data_dir, "BirthsAndFertilityRatesAnnual.csv"))
lfpr_wide <- read_singstat_wide(file.path(data_dir, "M182201.csv"))

asfr_by_age <- fertility_wide |>
  mutate(age_group = standardise_age_group(data_series)) |>
  filter(age_group %in% age_groups) |>
  to_long_years() |>
  transmute(
    year,
    age_group = factor(age_group, levels = age_groups),
    asfr = value
  ) |>
  filter(year >= 1980, !is.na(asfr)) |>
  arrange(age_group, year)

tfr_annual <- fertility_wide |>
  filter(data_series == "Total Fertility Rate (TFR)") |>
  to_long_years() |>
  transmute(year, tfr = value)

lfpr_female <- lfpr_wide |>
  mutate(
    section = case_when(
      data_series == "Female Resident Participation Rate" ~ "Female",
      data_series %in% c(
        "Total Resident Participation Rate",
        "Male Resident Participation Rate"
      ) ~ "Other",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  tidyr::fill(section, .direction = "down") |>
  filter(section == "Female", data_series != "Female Resident Participation Rate") |>
  mutate(age_group = standardise_age_group(data_series)) |>
  filter(age_group %in% age_groups) |>
  to_long_years() |>
  transmute(
    year,
    age_group = factor(age_group, levels = age_groups),
    female_lfpr_pct = value
  ) |>
  filter(year >= 1990, !is.na(female_lfpr_pct)) |>
  arrange(age_group, year)

recession_events <- tibble(
  recession = c(
    "1985 recession",
    "Asian Financial Crisis",
    "Global Financial Crisis",
    "COVID-19 recession"
  ),
  year = c(1985, 1998, 2009, 2020)
) |>
  mutate(xmin = year - 0.55, xmax = year + 0.55)

birth_policy_events <- tibble(
  year = c(1984, 1987, 2001, 2004, 2008, 2013),
  policy = c(
    "Graduate Mothers Scheme",
    "Have Three or More policy",
    "Baby Bonus",
    "M&P Package",
    "Enhanced M&P Package",
    "Enhanced M&P Package"
  ),
  label_level = c(1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2)
)

asfr_total_by_year <- asfr_by_age |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(total_asfr = sum(asfr, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

lfpr_scale <- max(asfr_total_by_year$total_asfr, na.rm = TRUE) / 100

lfpr_line <- lfpr_female |>
  filter(year >= min(asfr_by_age$year), year <= max(asfr_by_age$year))

  ) +

    linetype = "dotted",
    linewidth = 0.75,
    colour = "black"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = birth_policy_events,
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = Inf,
      label = paste0(year, ": ", policy),
      vjust = if_else(label_level == 1, 1.25, 2.65)
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    angle = 90,
    hjust = 1,
    size = 3,
    colour = "black"
  ) +
  geom_col(
    data = asfr_by_age,
    aes(x = year, y = asfr, fill = age_group),
    width = 0.82,
    alpha = 0.68
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = lfpr_line,
    aes(x = year, y = female_lfpr_pct * lfpr_scale, group = age_group),
    colour = "ghostwhite",
    linewidth = 2.1,
    lineend = "round"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = lfpr_line,
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = female_lfpr_pct * lfpr_scale,
      colour = age_group,
      group = age_group
    ),
    linewidth = 1.15,
    linetype = "dashed",
    alpha = 0.98,
    lineend = "round"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(1980, 2025.6),

  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(

      ~ . / lfpr_scale,

  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(

  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = age_group_colours,
    name = "Age group",
    labels = function(x) str_remove(x, " Years")
  ) +
  guides(
    fill = guide_legend(title = "Age group", order = 1, nrow = 1),
    colour = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Singapore fertility and female labour-force participation by age group",
    subtitle = "Stacked bars show ASFR by age group. Dashed lines show female LFPR. Shaded bands mark recessions; dotted lines mark major policies.",
    x = "Year",
    caption = "Associations shown, not causation."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9.5),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 7.5, colour = "grey40"),
    legend.position = "bottom",

grads <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "M850581_female_university_qualified.csv"))

age_band_stops <- tibble(
  midpoint = c(17, 22, 27, 32, 37, 42, 47),
  colour = c("#D73027", "#FC8D59", "#FEE08B", "#A6D96A", "#1A9850", "#4575B4", "#762A83")
)

age_colour_ramp <- colorRamp(age_band_stops$colour, space = "Lab")

birth_age_to_colour <- function(age) {
  t <- approx(
    age_band_stops$midpoint,
    seq(0, 1, length.out = nrow(age_band_stops)),
    xout = age,
    rule = 2
  )$y
  cols <- age_colour_ramp(t)
  rgb(cols[, 1], cols[, 2], cols[, 3], maxColorValue = 255)
}

literacy_raw <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_dir, "IndicatorsOnEducationAndLiteracyAnnual.csv"),

)
literacy <- literacy_raw |>
  filter(str_detect(DataSeries, "^\\s*Literacy Rate \\(15 Years & Over\\) - (Males|Females)\\s*$")) |>
  mutate(sex = if_else(str_detect(DataSeries, "Males"), "male_literacy_pct", "female_literacy_pct")) |>
  select(-DataSeries) |>
  pivot_longer(-sex, names_to = "year", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(year), value = as.numeric(value)) |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = value) |>
  arrange(year)

family_size_wide <- read_singstat_wide(file.path(data_dir, "ResidentEverMarriedFemalesByAgeGroupAndNumberOfChildrenBornAnnual.csv"))
cpi_wide <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(data_dir, "ConsumerPriceIndexCPI2024AsBaseYearMonthly.csv"),
  na = c("", "na", "NA", "N.A.", "-"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  rename(data_series = DataSeries)

cpi_annual <- cpi_wide |>
  filter(data_series == "All Items") |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = matches("^\\d{4}[A-Za-z]{3}$"),
    names_to = "period",
    values_to = "cpi_index"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(str_sub(period, 1, 4)),
    cpi_index = readr::parse_number(as.character(cpi_index))
  ) |>
  filter(year >= 1990, year <= 2025) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(cpi_index = mean(cpi_index, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

family_size_tagged <- family_size_wide |>
  mutate(
    age_group = if_else(str_detect(data_series, "^\\d+\\s*-\\s*\\d+\\s+Years$"), data_series, NA_character_),
    children_born = case_when(
      data_series == "None" ~ "None",
      data_series == "1 Child" ~ "1 child",
      data_series == "2 Children" ~ "2 children",
      data_series %in% c("3 Children", "4 Or More Children", "3 Or More Children") ~ "3 or more children",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  tidyr::fill(age_group, .direction = "down")

family_size_40_49 <- family_size_tagged |>
  filter(str_detect(age_group, "^40\\s*-\\s*49"), !is.na(children_born)) |>
  to_long_years() |>
  transmute(year, children_born, females = value) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(
    total_females = sum(females, na.rm = TRUE),
    share_pct = females / total_females * 100
  ) |>
  ungroup()

family_size_selected <- family_size_40_49 |>
  filter(year %in% c(1990, 2000, 2010, 2020, 2025)) |>
  group_by(year, children_born) |>
  summarise(share_pct = sum(share_pct, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    children_born = factor(
      children_born,
      levels = c("3 or more children", "2 children", "1 child", "None")
    ),
    label = if_else(share_pct >= 7, paste0(round(share_pct, 0), "%"), "")
  )

cpi_selected <- cpi_annual |>
  filter(year %in% c(1990, 2000, 2010, 2020, 2025)) |>
  arrange(year) |>
  mutate(
    cost_step_pct = (cpi_index / lag(cpi_index) - 1) * 100,
    cost_fill_pct = replace_na(cost_step_pct, 0),
    cost_label = if_else(
      year == 1990,
      "Cost baseline",
      paste0("+", round(cost_step_pct), "% cost")
    )
  )

policy_events <- tribble(
  ~event_year, ~event_label, ~policy_stance,
  1972, "Stop at Two", "Anti-natalist",
  1987, "Have Three or More", "Pro-natalist",
  2001, "Baby Bonus", "Pro-natalist",
  2013, "Marriage and Parenthood package", "Pro-natalist"
)

economic_shocks <- tribble(
  ~shock_year, ~shock_label, ~severity, ~quarters_below_peak,
  1985, "1985", "Severe", 6,
  1998, "1998", "Severe", 6,
  2001, "2001", "Moderate", 5,
  2009, "2009", "Most severe", 6,
  2020, "2020", "Most severe", 4
)

policy_window <- policy_events |>
  crossing(relative_year = -5:10) |>
  mutate(year = event_year + relative_year) |>
  left_join(tfr_annual, by = "year") |>
  mutate(
    event_label = factor(
      event_label,
      levels = c("Stop at Two", "Have Three or More", "Baby Bonus", "Marriage and Parenthood package")
    )
  )

shock_window <- policy_events |>
  crossing(economic_shocks) |>
  mutate(
    relative_year = shock_year - event_year,
    recovery_years = quarters_below_peak / 4,
    relative_recovery_end = relative_year + recovery_years,
    event_label = factor(
      event_label,
      levels = c("Stop at Two", "Have Three or More", "Baby Bonus", "Marriage and Parenthood package")
    )
  ) |>
  filter(relative_year <= 10, relative_recovery_end >= -5) |>
  mutate(
    xmin = pmax(relative_year, -5),
    xmax = pmin(relative_recovery_end, 10)
  )

  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-5, 0, 5, 10)) +
  labs(
    title = "Did recessions and policies explain fertility changes?",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = policy year. Shaded bands show economic recovery duration and recession severity.",
    x = "Years from policy",
    y = "TFR",
    colour = "Policy stance",
    fill = "Economic shock severity",
    caption = "Policy and recession markers provide context only. Timing is not causal proof."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

## The Story {#the-story .section-divider background-image="images/story-bg.jpg" background-size="cover" background-position="center" background-opacity="0.5"}

::: section-number
01
:::

::: divider-title
The Story
:::

::: divider-subtitle
Singapore's fertility decline is not only about fewer births. It is also
about who is giving birth, when family formation happens and whether
policies coincide with recovery.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What question are we answering? {.story-slide}

::: kicker
Research focus
:::

::: story-big
Why has Singapore's fertility rate kept falling despite policy
attention?
:::

::: story-sub
Our answer is descriptive, not causal: the decline appears alongside
later family formation, changing education and labour-force patterns,
smaller completed families and uneven policy or recession timing.
:::

::: story-question
<strong>Main question:</strong> What demographic and social changes are
associated with Singapore's persistently low fertility from 1980 to
2025?
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: divider-title

## Insight 1: Education, LFPR and birth timing {.clean-slide}

::::: {.two-col .plot-wide}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.8
#| fig-height: 5.2
p_insight1
```

:::: side-note
::: kicker
Insight 1
:::

<h3>What is driving the increase in female LFPR?</h3>

<p>The number of female LFPR increasing greatly from 50% in 1990 to 60% in 2025.</p>

<p>The same period also shows the stark increase in the number of female university graduates over three decades.</p>

<p>Over the same period also shows the number of median age at first birth rising from 28 years in 1990 to 32 years in 2025.</p>

<p><strong>Interpretation:</strong> Female LFPR in Singapore rose as a result of rising educational attainment [1]. This shift in cultural norm is causing later marriages, since more women are spending time pursuing higher education and establishing their careers [2].</p>
::::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Insight 2: Longer schooling and younger-age fertility {.clean-slide}

::::: {.two-col .plot-wide}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.8
#| fig-height: 5.2
p_insight2
```

:::: side-note
::: kicker
Insight 2
:::

<h3>Women literacy rates in Singapore</h3>

<p>Government policies drove female literacy rates up. 1961: Free primary education was offered. 1994: School curriculum was unified for all sexes. 2003: Quote for female intake to NUS medical school lifted.</p>

<p>With more equal opportunities, women are now spending more time in school, pursuing higher levels of education.</p>

<p>Therefore, the female LFPR for ages ranged 15-19 and 20-24 have dropped because girls at that age are still schooling and hence, not able to join the workforce.</p>

<p><strong>Interpretation:</strong> Education once went to sons; women were confined to labour or homemaking. Women now pursue higher education and delay starting a family, extending the same pattern of later labour force entry seen across this period.</p>
::::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Insight 3: Completed family size became smaller {.clean-slide}

::::: {.two-col .plot-wide}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 5.5
p_insight3b
```

:::: side-note
::: kicker
Insight 3
:::

<h3>Later family formation connects to smaller completed families</h3>

<p>Among ever-married women aged 40 to 49, larger families became less
common.</p>

<p>Smaller family-size categories became more prominent over time.</p>

<p>Rising consumer price index over the years shows the increasing cost of living.</p>

<p><strong>Interpretation:</strong> Because when women are more focused on pursuing higher levels of education and establishing careers, they will start families at a later age. At that age, they might not be as fertile to have many children. Moreover, the rising cost of living acts as a disincentive for families to have lesser children because its financially unsustainable. </p>
::::
:::::

:::: side-note
::: kicker
Insight 4
:::

<h3>Policy and recession timing give context</h3>

<p>Some policy periods coincide with short-term changes, but no
sustained recovery appears.</p>

<p>Recession bands help show economic timing around policy windows.</p>

<p><strong>Interpretation:</strong> The policies introduced by the government have limited effectiveness. Some of its effectiveness may be compromised due to the enticing financial incentives during periods of economic downturn. </p>

## Limitations {.clean-slide}

::: kicker
Interpretation boundaries
:::

<h2>What we can and cannot claim</h2>

::: hr-accent
:::

:::::: limit-grid
::: limit-card
<h3>Association, not causation</h3>

<p>Policies, recessions and social indicators are used as timing
context. They do not prove a direct cause.</p>
:::

::: limit-card
<h3>Different measures</h3>

<p>ASFR, TFR, LFPR, education and age measures use different units, so
we avoid forcing them onto one scale unless clearly labelled.</p>
:::

::: limit-card
<h3>Period versus cohort</h3>

<p>TFR describes fertility in a year, while completed family size
describes older cohorts. Both are useful, but they answer different
questions.</p>
:::
::::::

::: divider-title
Conclusion

::: divider-subtitle
What the whole story means for fertility decline.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Conclusion {#conclusion .clean-slide}

::: kicker
Final takeaway
:::

::: conclusion-big
Singapore's fertility decline appears to be a long-term structural
pattern, not a drop caused by one isolated policy, recession or
demographic change.
:::

::: story-question
The clearest story is cumulative: younger-age fertility weakened, female
education and LFPR rose, family formation shifted later and completed
families became smaller. Policy matters, but it operates within these
broader social and demographic shifts.
:::
